What you are describing is called the psychology of unemployment - although a more accurate description might be the psychology of being inactive. It is a very real and well documented phenomenon that the government does not like to talk about. Employment counselors know all about it and have designed proven group programs that break an unemployed person out of the pattern and often return them to the workforce. Although these programs do work and enjoy a high success rate, they also cost money to operate and the government does not like spending this additional money on these types of programs.

The psychology of unemployment is a dangerous situation that leads to further and deeper psychological phenomenon that become much more difficult to treat... requiring much more intensive and longer term programs to address. The simple fact is there are many many people who are too far gone and cannot ever be returned to the workforce in any capacity. The government does not like to talk about them either.

A quick cure is volunteer employment - if you cannot find work, or are no longer in the workforce, then do charity stuff - it's mostly the same as real work, sometimes it is real work, you just don't get paid:) You do get all of the other social benefits associated with group activity, and sometimes you do get paid after all. Charity work often leads right back to real employment. At the very least it gets you out of the bed in the morning, dressed and on the road, and you are spending time with people, doing stuff, and working towards some form of goal - all of which is actually very good for your physical health and mental state of mind. We are designed to be social creatures. We are also designed to work.

Social networking does seem to substitute somewhat for the social needs normally met through actual human interaction - but you can also see people going quite mad on the social networks over time:) It's not quite the same as the real deal.

My grandfather retired and then joined his local government. He takes that job very seriously and helped them claw their way out from debt the past 20 years. He plays tennis twice a week and works out the other three days, playing against men 20 years younger than him.

Lastly, knowing that he's 87 and going to die soon, he's begun to prioritize family. He is constantly reaching out to his grandchildren and children to meet for dinner, plan trips, and wants to be remembered and loved when he's gone by all of them.

Retirement is what you make it. You can take the time to join causes you believe in and volunteering to leave the world better than you arrived, or you can lounge about and just slowly fade into your grave. As long as you try to have a strong family unit, good hobbies, and try to keep your body healthy retirement sounds amazing to me and I look forward to seeing what my life is like when I reach that point.

The problem with unemployment for me, in my experience, is that you have all this "free" time but absolutely no money. The only things you can do when you have no money and have to ration your fuel consumption are things like walking around... Everything in America costs money. UBI addresses this because it gives people enough money in a consistent way such that they don't have to waste time thinking about what THEY HAVE TO DO TO SURVIVE and instead can focus on finding things that give their life meaning.

The point of a UBI is not to simply sit at home eating Cheetos. I'm sure some people will do that, but then again some people already do, far too many even. The real kicker with UBI and the paradigm that creates... well if corruption doesn't pervert it like it did Capitalism... is that it leads to a future where there literally are only enough jobs for around 1/3 of the population. After a few generations of UBI we'll live in a world where people are on waiting lists with a 3 month ON and 9 month OFF work rotation.
